0. FOREWORD
0.1 This
Indian Standard ( First Revision ) was ndopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 31 January 1985, after the draft finalized by the Precious Metals Sectional Committee had been approved by the Structural and Metals Division Council.

0.2 In modern dentistry, wire is the principal form in which wrought metal is used. Gold alloys used for such wires are complex alloys consilver, copper, zinc and sometimes taining gold, platinum, palladium, Gold alloy wires are occasionally employed for the construction nickel. of clasps and are also used for the construction of orthodontic appliances. In order that the wire should perform good service, it is necessary that it should have proper composition and tensile properties. 0.2.1 Two types of alloys for making dental wire have been specified. Typical compositions of gold alloys along with their physical properties Fusion temperature ranges have have been included in Appendix A. also been indicated for these typical alloys. 0.3 The following a) b) standard was first published modifications have been made: MKS units have been changed in 1966. 8. SIZES OF WIRE 8.1 The nominal wire size shall be designated
by the diameter expressed in millimetres. The dimension of the wire shall be subject to the tolerThe range of the nominal ance of f3 percent on the nominal size. sizes should be taken from an arithmetic series of dimensions starting from 0.5 mm and having a common difference of 0.1 mm. NOTE - Subsequent consideration will be given to the introduction of the preferred range of sizes when further experience has been gained in the use of sizes specified above.

or its container shall be legibly marked with the type of the alloy; size; mass of the contents; and the *me, initials or trademark of the manufacturer. 5

11.2 Visual inspection requirements specified

11.3 In case a test specimen fails to meet the physical requirements, more specimens shall be tested. The material shall be considered factory only if both retest specimens satisfy the requirements.

11.4 The sample for chemical analysis shall consist of a composite sample of ten grams of each lot of 200 g or fraction thereof. Sample for this purpose shall be taken by shearing or clipping pieces from the entire remelting in a clean container at a temperature slightly cross-sections, above the melting range mixing thoroughly and pouring into cold mould of convenient size. The sample so prepared shall be milled, drilled or sawed in such a manner as to represent the entire cross-section. Saw, drill or any other tool used shall be thoroughly clean and no lubricant shall be used in the operation. 12. TESTING

12.1 Tensile Testing - For the purpose of tensile testing ( see Appendix B ), test specimen of the dental gold alloy wire shall be of round crosssection of 1.0 + 0.2 mm diameter. The proof stress and percentage elongation shall be determined on a gauge length of 50 mm. The test specimens shall be heat-treated before testing. This shall be done by placing the specimens in a furnace at 810�C for Type 1 alloys and 700�C for Type 2 alloys for ten minutes and immediately quenching in water at room temperature.

APPENDIX B 0 Clauses 7.1 and 12.1 )
METHOD B-l. FOR DETERMINATION OF DENTAL GOLD OF TENSILE ALLOY WIRE PROOF PROPERTIES STRESS

DETERMINATION

OF O-1 PERCENT

B-l.1 Increasing loads should be applied successively to the hardened specimen and maintained in each case for ten seconds. After removal of each load, the permanent elongation which the specimen has taken should be measured. The test should be stopped when the elongation exceeds 0.1 percent. B-l.2 An accurate curve should be plotted by taking loads as ordinates and corresponding elongation as abscissae. A straight line should be drawn on the graph parallel to the straight part of the curve at a distance from the straight part measured along the given axis of the abscissae equal to 0.1 percent of the initial gauge length ( Fig. 1 ). The desired stress will correspond to the point of intersection of straight line and the curve.
